# Seahaven benchmark: latest results

> **Sections 1-6 predate this repository's current environment; section 7 does not.** Sections 1-6
> were measured on CPython **3.14.0rc2** with a hand-patched `pydantic` 2.12.3 in place of the
> locked 2.13.5 -- the only way the suite ran at the time -- as the Environment table below
> records. The repository now builds on a final 3.14 against the lock, unpatched, so these figures
> are not comparable with a run made today and re-running the benchmark is a maintainer's call.
> Everything under "What these numbers are, and what they are not" applies on top of this. Section
> 7 was measured separately on 2026-09-14 against the lock, and carries its own provenance line.

Generated by `uv run --no-sync python -m bench all --out bench/results/latest.md --force` in 448 s. Everything above the
`## Reading` heading is generated; the reading below it was written by hand from these tables.

## What these numbers are, and what they are not

**They are one machine, one afternoon.** The run below happened inside a shared, virtualised
sandbox: a few vCPUs of a host we do not own, no CPU pinning, no control over what else was
running, and a filesystem nobody would deploy on. Every figure carries the spread of its own
repeats; differences smaller than that spread are noise, and this document rounds everything to
two significant figures because a third would be a fiction.

**Use them for:** the order of magnitude of a call; the *shape* of a curve (what happens to
throughput and to waiting as the concurrency gate changes); and comparison against another run of
this same harness on this same machine -- which is how a regression is found.

**Do not use them for:** capacity planning, hardware comparison, a service-level objective, a
claim in a README, or a comparison with any other framework's benchmark. The latency columns come
from a closed loop with no think time: every session issues its next call the instant the last
returns, so the process is saturated throughout and the percentiles are the queueing of that
offered load. They are not what a session would see on a server that is not saturated.

**This is never a gate.** The benchmark is not in CI, nothing fails on a number, and no threshold
is asserted anywhere. `tests/test_bench.py` proves the harness still runs; it does not check a
speed.

**What "cold" can mean here.** A cold run drops each instance's pages from this guest's
page cache with `posix_fadvise(DONTNEED)`. The host's cache and the hypervisor's are not ours to
drop, so a cold read here is a read that missed *this* machine's cache and may well have been
served by one below it. Treat the cold figures as a floor on how fast cold can be, not as a
measurement of a cold disk.

## Method

**The world.** ProjectTracker `agency`, the framework's largest fixture: twelve people, nine
projects, six hundred issues with six months of history. Every call goes through
`Instance.call`, which is the path an eval takes -- argument validation, the middleware chain,
the per-call transaction, the tool, the changeset session, the serialiser.

**The workloads.**

- **`read`**: get_issue by id, walking the fixture's 600 issues in a seeded shuffle: a pass of 600 calls drives every issue exactly once, a shorter pass the first N of the shuffle, a longer one wraps
- **`write_mix`**: create_issue, add_comment, transition_issue, assign_issue, in that cycle

**One instance per session.** An instance serialises its own calls under its lock, so every
worker thread gets its own instance -- a private copy of the fixture, which is how OpenEnv
serves sessions.

**Warm and cold.** *Warm* means the session has already served one full pass of its workload,
so its connection's page cache holds what the pass touches. *Cold* means the instance has served
nothing and its files have been evicted from this guest's page cache. Both are measured with a
fixed number of calls per session, so two passes of one configuration do identical work.

**The write mix's warm and cold columns differ by more than a cache.** Its warm-up writes as many
rows as the measured pass will, so a warm write pass runs on an instance carrying a pass worth of
extra rows and changeset entries while a cold one runs on a virgin instance. An instance's write
cost climbs with those rows by roughly the size of the gap between the two columns, so the write
mix's cold/warm axis mixes cache state with accumulated state and should not be read as a cache
effect. The read workload has no such confound: it writes nothing.

**Logging.** The `seahaven` logger is pinned to WARNING for the run, so the one INFO line every
call emits costs a level check and nothing else. Under `seahaven serve`, uvicorn configures INFO
handlers and that line is formatted and written; this benchmark does not measure that.

**The gate sweep.** Gate sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 0 (`0` is no gate, the control) x offered load 4,
32 sessions x cache warm, cold x workload `read`, `write_mix`, 3 repeats, 200 calls per session
per pass, seed 11. The gate is set through `seahaven.instances.set_concurrency`, which is what
`seahaven serve --concurrency` calls. Each repeat is a whole pass over every point in a seeded
shuffle, so drift over the 386 s the sweep took is spread across the configurations rather than
handed to whichever ran last.

**Reproducing it.** From the repository root, on the commit named above:

```
uv run --no-sync python -m bench all --out bench/results/latest.md --force
```

## 1. Baseline: one session, one thread

What a call costs with nothing else running. `functional_spec.md` §23 asks for "about 3,000
one-row reads per second per process"; the `read` rows are that number.

| Workload | Cache | Calls/pass | Calls/s | min-max | p50 | p95 | worst |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `read` | warm | 600 | 9.1k | 8.3k-9.1k | 0.10 ms | 0.17 ms | 0.30 ms |
| `read` | cold | 600 | 7.9k | 7.7k-8.2k | 0.10 ms | 0.24 ms | 0.84 ms |
| `write_mix` | warm | 600 | 2.0k | 2.0k-2.1k | 0.36 ms | 0.54 ms | 14 ms |
| `write_mix` | cold | 600 | 2.1k | 2.0k-2.1k | 0.35 ms | 0.56 ms | 14 ms |

Latencies are per call, in milliseconds, pooled over the repeats.

## 2. Where a one-row read goes

The same `get_issue`, on one instance, driving the same rows in the same order, warm, timed three
ways: through `Instance.call`; as the two statements the tool runs (the issue's row, then its
labels) through `Db.rows`, which is the data layer world code is handed; and as those same two
statements stepped straight on the APSW cursor.

| | Per call | Share of the call |
|---|---:|---:|
| Through `Instance.call` | 0.11 ms | 100% |
| The two statements through `Db.rows` | 0.022 ms | ~20% |
| The same two statements on the APSW cursor | 0.012 ms | ~11% |

The middle row is **not** SQLite's share: `Db.rows` is framework code -- an error-translating
context manager, and a dict built per row from the cursor description -- so counting it as SQLite
would book half the data layer to the database. The bottom row is the closest this can get to
SQLite proper, and it is still an upper bound: the statements are stepped on the inspection
connection, whose read-only authorizer runs a Python callback while SQLite prepares them.

What this supports is §23's "the framework layer, not SQLite, as the per-call cost": about 89%
of a one-row read is Seahaven, of which roughly 9 points are the data layer and the rest is
dispatch. From 1800 calls down each leg.

## 3. The gate sweep

One table per workload and cache state. **Calls/s** is the whole process: every session's calls
over the pass's wall time. **spread** is (max - min) / median over the repeats -- this cell's own
noise. **worst** is the longest any single call waited.

Two things these tables cannot show. **Fairness**, except through `worst`: every session is given
the same number of calls, so a pass does not end until the worst-served one has had all of them,
and a count per session would read the same at every gate size. Section 4, which is bounded by
time rather than by calls, is where unfairness is visible. And **`Calls/s` and `worst` are not
independent**: a pass ends when its slowest session finishes, so a configuration that leaves one
session waiting also spends the tail of its pass below full load, which lowers the rate of exactly
the configurations that score badly on waiting.

## 4. One slow call, 4 ordinary sessions

4 sessions reading one row at a time, beside one session looping a slow `run_sql` self-join, for
3.0 s at each gate size, 3 times over. The question a sweep of short calls cannot ask: what a
gate size does to everybody else when one call is slow.

| Gate | Reader calls/s | p50 | p95 | worst | calls per reader | Slow calls/s | Slow p50 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 4.2k | 0.22 ms | 0.34 ms | 3.1k ms | 1-12874 | 0.33 | 3.1k ms |
| 2 | 3.4k | 0.25 ms | 1.2 ms | 3.0k ms | 1-5351 | 0.33 | 73 ms |
| 4 | 3.8k | 0.59 ms | 2.5 ms | 3.0k ms | 1-4011 | 13 | 76 ms |
| 8 | 3.6k | 0.69 ms | 3.3 ms | 19 ms | 2659-2816 | 13 | 78 ms |
| 16 | 3.7k | 0.69 ms | 3.2 ms | 18 ms | 2737-2817 | 13 | 77 ms |
| none | 3.9k | 0.69 ms | 2.8 ms | 15 ms | 2916-3044 | 13 | 77 ms |

"calls per reader" is the worst-served and best-served reader **within one window** -- the window
in which the worst-served reader did least, out of the repeats -- so the two counts are two
sessions that really were running side by side. It is what this section exists for: the rate and
the quantiles average over readers that were served and readers that were not.

Both rate columns are divided by a window that includes the drain after it closes -- a caller
blocked on the gate when the window ends still has to take a slot and run before it can stop --
which understates them by a few percent, most at the gate sizes that make callers wait. The counts
per reader are unaffected.

## 5. Repeatability, and the noise floor

Each cell was measured 3 times, in a different order each pass.

| | |
|---|---|
| Median spread across cells | 7% |
| Worst spread | 20% (read, cold, 4 sessions, gate 2) |
| Drift check | `read, warm, 4 sessions, gate none`: 3.8k at 72 s → 4.1k at 204 s → 4.0k at 289 s |

The drift check is one configuration's passes in the order they ran, spread through the sweep.
Half the cells moved by more than the median, so the median is a floor on this machine's noise and
not a threshold: a difference between two cells smaller than the median is not a difference this
machine can see at all, and one smaller than the worst spread above deserves no weight without
more repeats than this run had.

## 7. A composite tree: what a node costs

> **Provenance.** These tables were measured by `uv run python -m bench composite` at
> 2026-09-14T09:14:58+00:00, commit 708ead4 (working tree modified), Python 3.14.7 (CPython, with
> the GIL), on Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.80GHz. This section carries its own machine because
> it can be regenerated on its own, and the rest of this document may come from a different run.

`architecture.md` §15 says an idle composite instance is N stores, N connections and N sessions,
and that until this section the benchmark measured one node per instance, a figure read as a
per-node floor. Every other measurement here is that one node. These two tables are the floor
itself, measured on the committed composite tree of `tests/worlds/README.md`: `payments` is a
leaf of one node, `shop` adds it, and `emporium` adds `payments` twice -- once under a scope --
and `shop`, sealing to the four nodes `main`, `payments`, `payments_eu` and `shop`, with
`shop/payments` an alias of `payments` rather than a fifth store.

**These are the smallest worlds in the repository**, and that is what makes them a floor: a
`payments` node is one table and two tools, so what is measured here is close to what an *empty*
node costs. It is the wrong shape for a typical store -- a node carrying a real schema costs that
schema on top of every figure below, and the write rows here are one row into a four-column table
with no index but its primary key.

### Standing one up

Each tree sealed, opened, measured and destroyed 5 times, after one discarded open and destroy:
a tree's first open in a process costs several milliseconds more than its steady state, and
timing it would fill the min-max columns with that rather than with the pass-to-pass spread they
are read as. Every timing is the median of the measured passes and each min-max is its own
column's spread over them. **Stores** is the databases on disk and **Files** is everything the
instance directory holds -- each store plus the `-wal` and `-shm` SQLite keeps beside it -- both
counted off a live instance rather than derived from the node count, because "N files" is the
claim under test. **Idle on disk** is that directory before the instance has served a single
call. A **seal** is forced by `composition.bump()`, which is what every registration verb calls,
so each one is a whole walk of the tree and not a cache hit.

| Tree | Nodes | Stores | Files | Idle on disk | Seal | Open | min-max | Destroy | min-max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|
| `payments` | 1 | 1 | 3 | 44 KiB | 0.029 ms | 4.0 ms | 3.0 ms-7.4 ms | 0.26 ms | 0.18 ms-0.35 ms |
| `shop` | 2 | 2 | 6 | 88 KiB | 0.041 ms | 6.4 ms | 5.8 ms-6.8 ms | 0.29 ms | 0.27 ms-0.36 ms |
| `emporium` | 4 | 4 | 12 | 176 KiB | 0.090 ms | 13 ms | 12 ms-14 ms | 0.59 ms | 0.54 ms-0.63 ms |

Against the one-node leaf, which opens in 4.0 ms and holds 44 KiB:

- **`shop`** is one node more than the leaf: +2.4 ms to open, +44 KiB on disk, +0.034 ms to
  destroy.
- **`emporium`** is 3 nodes more than the leaf: +9.0 ms to open, +132 KiB on disk, +0.32 ms to
  destroy (3.0 ms and 44 KiB per added node).

### What a node costs a call

One thread, warm, 3 times over: a pass is 1000 calls on a fresh instance that has already served
one identical pass off the clock, which is `bench/runner.py`'s warm-up rule and is applied to
both trees alike. A repeat is a whole pass over every row of the table, so drift during the run
is spread across the rows rather than handed to whichever ran last -- which matters here, where
the difference being looked for is smaller than the machine's noise. The read is an account
holding exactly one charge, so every call of the pass returns one row. `settle_order` is the
composite's own: one call that places an order in `shop`, charges `payments` and writes the
host's own row, through two nested `handle.call`s.

| Call | Tree | Nodes | Calls/s | min-max | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|
| one-row read | `payments` | 1 | 15k | 15k-15k | 0.056 ms | 0.10 ms |
| one-row read | `emporium` | 4 | 14k | 14k-16k | 0.057 ms | 0.11 ms |
| one-row write | `payments` | 1 | 7.7k | 7.6k-7.8k | 0.092 ms | 0.17 ms |
| one-row write | `emporium` | 4 | 7.4k | 6.7k-7.8k | 0.096 ms | 0.20 ms |
| settle_order | `emporium` | 4 | 2.4k | 2.4k-2.5k | 0.30 ms | 0.55 ms |

- **one-row read**, the same tool at one node and at 4: 0.056 ms against 0.057 ms at the median,
  +0.00054 ms (1%) for 3 added nodes. The noisier of the two cells moved 14% in *rate* between
  its own repeats -- a proxy for this pair's noise, and not the same statistic as the pooled
  median being compared -- so the difference is smaller than this run's own noise and cannot be
  told from zero.
- **one-row write**, the same tool at one node and at 4: 0.092 ms against 0.096 ms at the
  median, +0.0044 ms (5%) for 3 added nodes. The noisier of the two cells moved 15% in *rate*
  between its own repeats -- a proxy for this pair's noise, and not the same statistic as the
  pooled median being compared -- so the difference is smaller than this run's own noise and
  cannot be told from zero.
- **settle_order** is 0.30 ms at the median against 0.096 ms for the one-row write on the same
  tree -- a fresh instance per pass, so the same tree and never the same instance: 3.2x the cost
  of one call, for three writes to three stores, three transactions and two nested dispatches.

### What this section does not measure

- **That a seal's cost is bounded.** `composition.resolve` folds a node reached along several routes
  into one entry rather than concatenating its tools once per route, which is what keeps a diamond
  of tens of nodes in milliseconds instead of tens of seconds. The largest committed tree is four
  nodes with one alias, and it seals in microseconds either way. The seal column is a number for a
  future run to be compared against, not evidence about that bound.
- **The cost of `World.composition()` on the call path.** Every dispatch reads it, so it is inside
  every cell of the per-call table, but its hit path is one load and one integer compare under no
  lock and nothing here can resolve that on its own. The leaf-against-composite rows are the only
  evidence this run offers about it.
- **Memory, and the connection and session counts.** One connection and one changeset session per
  node is what `instances.NodeRuntime` opens. What this section counts is *files*: the connections
  and the sessions are read off the code as before, paid for inside the Open column, and neither
  counted nor weighed here.
- **Concurrency, and cold caches.** One thread, warm, no gate sweep. A per-call cost is a
  single-threaded number for the reason section 1 gives, and a composite instance offers the gate no
  question the ProjectTracker sweep does not already ask.
- **A real node.** See the paragraph above the first table: these worlds are one table and two tools
  each, which is what makes the figures a floor.

## Reading

Written by hand from the tables above, in the phase that produced them
(`specs/projects/seahaven_framework/phase_plans/phase_11.md`). The decision rule it applies was
written before the committed harness ran, by someone who had already scouted the shape of the
results with throwaway scripts. That plan says what can and cannot be claimed about that ordering;
read the rule as a judgement stated in advance, not as an independent yardstick.

Two bases are used below and they are not interchangeable. "The default runs at 73-82% of `n = 1`"
and "`n = 1` runs 22-37% more calls a second than the default" are the same eight rows of section 6
seen from either end; the first is the default's share of `n = 1`, the second is what `n = 1` adds
to the default. Where a sentence says which value it is a percentage *of*, it means that one.

### Confirmed

**`functional_spec.md` §23's baseline holds.** One-row reads run at 9.1k/s in a single-threaded
process, warm, and 7.9k/s cold. Saturated -- 32 sessions all calling at once -- the process still
does 2.9k-4.3k/s depending on the gate. §23 asks for "about 3,000 one-row reads per second per
process" and this machine clears it everywhere but one cell: the current gate default with 32
sessions on a cold cache reads 2.9k/s, just under. That is the only read cell of the sweep below
3,000, it is under by less than this machine's noise, and it is quoted here because a baseline
this run met in 23 cells and missed in one should say so rather than round the one away.

**§23's "the framework layer, not SQLite, as the per-call cost" holds, and so does §5.2's estimate
of SQLite's share.** A one-row read is 0.11 ms through `Instance.call` and 0.012 ms when its two
statements are stepped straight on the APSW cursor: about 89% of the call is Seahaven. §5.2 says
"SQLite is about 7% of a call"; 11% is an upper bound on the same quantity, because the cursor leg
still pays for the inspection connection's authorizer, so this run supports that sentence rather
than contradicting it. The middle leg -- 20% through `Db.rows` -- is the data layer, not SQLite:
of a call, roughly 11 points are the statements themselves, 9 more are `Db`'s wrapper, and the
remaining 80 are dispatch, validation, the chain, the transaction and the serialiser.

### Not confirmed

**`architecture.md` §5.2's "`n` near the core count is the measured throughput optimum" is false on
this build.** There is no optimum at the core count. Throughput is highest at `n = 1` in every row
of the sweep -- both workloads, both cache states, both offered loads -- and the default (4 here,
the process's cpu count) runs at 73-82% of it, giving up 18-27% of the throughput `n = 1` reaches.
This is what a GIL build does: about 89% of a call is Python, so a second runnable thread adds
contention and no parallelism, and the semaphore's own acquire and release are paid per call on
top. A free-threaded build would answer differently, and nothing here says what it would answer.

### The gate default: unchanged, its stated reasons corrected

Under the rule fixed in the phase plan:

- **Rule 1.** `n = 1` runs 22-37% more calls a second than the default, in all eight rows. Every
  one of those gaps clears both the 7% median spread and the 20% the noisiest cell of this run
  moved, and the direction is the same in all eight. Real, not noise.
- **Rule 2** asks whether it is also no worse on waiting, *everywhere it was measured*. It is not,
  and the rejection rests on where it loses: at 4 sessions its worst observed wait is 146, 145, 431
  and 417 ms across the four workload and cache combinations, against the default's 20, 11, 33 and
  30 ms; and section 4 is decisive -- with one slow call in the process, the window in which
  `n = 1` served its worst reader least gave that reader **one call in three seconds** while
  another reader, in that same window, was served 12,874 times.

  Where it wins should be said too, because four generated rows say it. **At 32 sessions `n = 1`
  is better than the default on every axis, worst wait included**: 1.5k, 1.6k, 3.9k and 4.2k ms
  against the default's 1.9k, 2.1k, 4.7k and 4.6k, with a lower p50 and p95 in all four rows as
  well, direction consistent. Read the `worst` half of that with the same caution this document
  asks for elsewhere: `worst` is a single maximum with no spread of its own -- section 3's spread
  column is the rate's -- and the narrowest of those four gaps, 4.6 s against 4.2 s, is about 10%.
  What carries it is that all four rows point the same way, not any one of them. Rule 2 asks for
  "no worse everywhere" and one set of rows is enough to answer it, so the decision is unchanged --
  but "`n = 1` waits worse" is true of 4 sessions and of section 4, not of this machine under 32.
- **Rule 3** asks which value has the property a server needs -- no session waiting while others
  are served -- and the honest answer is that **no gate size has it**. The default does not: at
  gate 4 the same probe shows the same starved reader (**1 call** against 4,011 in one window), and
  at 32 sessions the default's worst wait is 1.9-4.7 s -- worse, in each of those four rows, than
  `n = 1`'s 1.5-4.2 s. Only gates that do not bind on the threads
  offered (8, 16, and no gate at all) served every reader evenly, and at 32 sessions, where 8 and
  16 do bind, they starve too. The unfairness is the semaphore's, not the number's, so rule 3
  elects nothing.
- **Rule 4** is therefore where this lands. **The default `min(os.process_cpu_count() or 4, 16)`
  stands, and the reasons recorded for it are corrected.** It is not the throughput optimum it was
  described as, and it is not fair either. One measured reason is left -- no value the sweep tried
  was better than this one on every axis at once -- and one design intent, recorded as an intent:
  following cpu affinity is the shape that keeps the free-threaded door open, and this run says
  nothing about what a free-threaded build would do. `instances.default_concurrency`'s docstring
  now says exactly that, unfairness included.

**The ungated control, scored against the default rather than left to prose.** `--concurrency 0`
is the one setting measured that served every reader evenly, and at 32 sessions it **matched or
beat** the default on throughput while cutting the worst wait by an order of magnitude: read/warm
3.7k against 3.2k and 155 ms against 1.9 s; read/cold 3.5k against 2.9k and 148 ms against 2.1 s;
write/warm 1.3k against 1.3k and 244 ms against 4.7 s; write/cold 1.3k against 1.3k and 212 ms
against 4.6 s. Two of those four are ties at this document's precision, and the two read rows are
16% and 21% apart -- one inside the 20% the noisiest cell of this run moved and the other barely
outside it -- so the throughput half of that sentence is "no worse", not "faster". The waiting
half is not close. It pays for it in p50 and p95 (read/warm/32: 2.2 ms and 34 ms, against the
default's 0.85 ms and 3.7 ms). Rule 2
therefore does not promote it -- and rule 4 could not have promoted it either, because `0` is not
a candidate for the default: `functional_spec.md` §13.1 defines the default as a gate size and `0`
as the operator's way to turn the gate off, so "ship without a gate" is a question for §13.1 and
not an outcome a tuning sweep can reach. The phase plan says this explicitly rather than leaving
it implied. What the sweep can say, and does, is that on this machine the gate costs throughput and
costs tail latency, and buys p50 and p95.

`architecture.md` §5.2's throughput-optimum sentence was left to the maintainer rather than edited
by the phase that measured it, because editing a `status: complete` artifact is a maintainer's call
in this repository and not a phase's. That call has since been made: §5.2 now states what this run
found, with a dated note pointing back here.

### The finding the sweep was not looking for

**A gate that binds starves somebody.** It is in the sweep's `worst` column -- at 32 sessions,
every gate from 1 to 16 has some call waiting 1.2-5.0 s while the median call of that same pass
is served in ten milliseconds or less, and the ungated process's worst wait is 148-244 ms -- and
section 4 shows it without ambiguity: at gates 1, 2 and 4, with five threads calling, a single
three-second window served one reader **once** and another one thousands of times. At gate 8 and
above, where the gate no longer binds on five threads, every reader got an even share (2,659 to
3,044 calls).

That is not the gate's size, and no value of `n` fixes it. It is `threading.BoundedSemaphore`: a
thread that releases a slot and immediately asks for another usually wins the race against the
waiter that was just woken, because the waiter needs the GIL to run and the barging thread already
has it. The gate never rejects a call -- `functional_spec.md` §13.1's promise that "calls queue and
nothing is rejected" is kept -- but a call that queues for seconds behind a thread barging in front
of it is not the service that sentence implies. A closed loop with no think time is the worst case
for it: a scouting run before this harness existed, with a millisecond of think time per session,
did not reproduce it, because a session that has gone away to do something else is not barging. That
observation is not one of the measurements above and is offered as a hint for whoever looks into it,
not as a result.

### For an operator

- `seahaven serve --concurrency` is the lever, and on this kind of hardware it is worth using --
  but measure your own world before turning it, because every option here trades one thing for
  another.
- `--concurrency 1` is the throughput and median-latency setting: 22-37% more calls a second than
  the default, and a p50 of 0.22 ms instead of 0.85 ms (read, warm, 32 sessions). At 32 sessions it
  is also the *better* setting for waiting -- its worst wait is below the default's in all four
  rows -- so this is not a throughput-for-latency trade at that scale.
- What `--concurrency 1` costs is the few-sessions case, and it costs it in the tail rather than
  the median. With four sessions its worst wait is 145-431 ms against the default's 11-33 ms, and
  in section 4 it produces the largest disparity of any gate size: one reader served once in three
  seconds while another was served 12,874 times. It is not uniquely bad there -- gates 2 and 4
  starve a reader to a single call in the same probe -- but it is the widest gap, and a one-slot
  gate is also the one that queues every reader behind each slow statement (76 ms at gate 4 in
  section 4; at gate 1 that statement itself waits, which is why its Slow p50 reads 3.1 s).
- `--concurrency 0` -- no gate -- was the most even setting measured, and at 32 sessions it cost
  nothing in throughput to get there. It pays in p50 and p95 under saturation.
- The default is the middle of these and the best at neither. Until slots are handed out in
  arrival order, a gate that binds on your offered load will leave somebody waiting, whatever
  number you give it.

### What this run cannot tell you

- **Cold cache barely registers here, and for the write mix it is not interpretable at all.** A
  single-threaded process runs about 13% fewer one-row reads a second cold than warm (7.9k against
  9.1k), and in the sweep the cold
  and warm tables rank the gate values the same way within the noise -- `n = 1` first everywhere,
  the rest of the values clustered inside a band this machine cannot resolve. `agency` is a 1.8 MB
  file on a fast virtual disk and this sandbox cannot evict the host's cache, so the argument that
  a larger `n` buys I/O overlap has not been tested by this run. The write mix's two columns differ
  by more than a cache besides -- its warm pass runs on an instance carrying a pass worth of extra
  rows, as the method section says -- so no cache conclusion should be drawn from them.
- **Throughput and waiting are not independent here.** A pass ends when its slowest session
  finishes, so a configuration that starves someone also runs the tail of its pass below full load.
  That depresses the `Calls/s` of exactly the configurations that score badly on `worst`. It makes
  the "`n = 1` is fastest" result conservative rather than flattering, but the two columns are
  projections of one phenomenon and any future re-reading of the sweep should treat them that way.
- **The noise floor is higher than the median.** The median cell moved 7% between repeats, but half
  of them moved more, and the worst moved 20%. The drift check re-measured one configuration three
  times through the run (3.8k, 4.1k, 4.0k; section 3 prints that cell's spread as 7%). The headline
  gaps (22-37%) clear the median and the worst; smaller claims in this document -- that the gates
  from 2 to 16 are much of a muchness on throughput, for instance -- sit inside that band and
  should be read as "no difference this machine can see" rather than as measurements.
- **One machine, four vCPUs, one build.** Nothing here is a hardware comparison, and the cap of 16
  in the default was never exercised: this process's default is 4.
- **The latency columns are saturation latencies**, from a closed loop with no think time. They are
  the queueing this benchmark offered, not a service level.

### The composite tree: what a node costs (section 7, added 2026-09-14)

Written from section 7 alone, in the phase that produced it
(`specs/projects/world_composition/phase_plans/phase_7.md`), and added to this document after the
rest of it existed. **That section was measured on its own run**, on a later day and a different
build -- CPython 3.14.7 against the lock, where every table above it is 3.14.0rc2 with a patched
`pydantic`, as the note at the top of this document says. Its provenance line carries that machine.
So do not read a figure of section 7 against a figure of sections 1-6: they share no machine state,
and `emporium` is not `agency`. Everything below is internal to that one run, a few seconds long
on one machine, with the per-call rows interleaved a row at a time and each tree's standing-up
passes run back to back.

**`architecture.md` §15's file count is exactly one store per node, and now it is counted rather
than assumed** -- the connections and the sessions of that same clause are not: one of each per
node is what `instances._open_node` opens, which is still read off the code and not off a table.
What section 7 counts is files: one database per node in all three trees (1, 2 and 4), and 3, 6
and 12 files once the `-wal` and `-shm` SQLite keeps beside each store are counted with them. An
idle node is 44 KiB on disk, the same figure in every tree.

**A node costs about 3 ms to open and about 0.1 ms to destroy.** The one-node leaf opens in 4.0 ms,
the two-node tree in 6.4 and the four-node tree in 13: +2.4 ms for `shop`'s one added node and +3.0
ms each for `emporium`'s three, after a discarded first open that would otherwise have paid a
work root that does not exist yet and a once-per-process sweep of abandoned directories into the
first figure of every row. Read those increments against the `Open` column's own min-max, which
is 3.0-7.4 ms on the leaf alone: "about 3 ms per node" is the claim, and this machine cannot
make it sharper than a millisecond or two. Destroying is +0.034 ms for `shop`'s one node and
+0.32 ms for `emporium`'s three (0.11 ms each), over min-max ranges of 0.18-0.35, 0.27-0.36 and
0.54-0.63 ms -- so the leaf-to-`shop` step sits inside the overlap of two cells and says
nothing, while the four-node tree is clear of the leaf by more than either spread. That is §15's
per-node floor: **roughly 3 ms and 44 KiB for an empty node**, with a store carrying a real
schema paying for that schema on top.

**A call costs what it costs, whatever the tree around it.** The same `list_charges` and
`create_charge`, driven on a one-node instance of `payments` and on the `payments` node of a
four-node `emporium`, differ by 1% and 5% at the median while the noisier cell of each pair moved
14% and 15% in rate between its own repeats. Three added nodes -- three more stores, connections
and changeset sessions -- buy no per-call cost this machine can see. It is what the code says
should happen (`call.py` opens the transaction of the one node that owns the tool, and
`World.composition()` is one load and one integer compare under no lock on the way in), and it
is the first measurement of it: an upper bound on composite dispatch at four nodes, not a proof
that it is zero.

**What a cross-node call costs is the nested dispatch, not the tree.** `settle_order` -- one agent
call that places an order in `shop`, charges `payments` and writes the host's own row through two
nested `handle.call`s -- is 0.30 ms against 0.096 ms for the single-store write on the same tree:
3.2x, for three writes to three stores in three transactions. A `handle.call` is priced like a call,
and a host tool that fans out to N stores should be budgeted as N calls.

**What it does not settle**, beyond the list section 7 prints for itself:

- **Nothing about many nodes.** The attach limit is 125 and this ladder stops at 4, so "3 ms per
  node" is measured over three added nodes. A tree near the bound would be a different measurement
  and would need a world built to be measured; nothing committed here has that shape.
- **Nothing about the seal at scale.** 0.029, 0.041 and 0.090 ms for one, two and four nodes is a
  whole walk of the tree every time, over a ladder far too short to say anything about the shape of
  the curve.
- **Nothing about memory or concurrency.** The connections and the changeset sessions are inside the
  Open column and were never counted or weighed on their own, and one thread with no gate says
  nothing about a server holding hundreds of composite instances -- which is the design target §15
  declines to re-derive.
